parts.name: The harbor square
parts.stand: In Manto Square on the harbor front, facing her bust.

paras.t: Welcome to Mykonos Town. Islanders call it Chora, which simply means the Town. And the larger-than-life bust in this square is the woman it's named for: Manto Mavrogenous, a heroine of the Greek War of Independence. She was extremely wealthy, and she gave her fortune to the cause.

A little background first. For almost three centuries, from 1537 to 1830, Mykonos was part of the Ottoman Empire. When the Greek Revolution broke out in 1821, this island played an important role, and Manto led it.

She was born in Trieste, in what's now Italy, and grew up educated: ancient Greek philosophy and history, and fluent French, Italian and Turkish. When the fighting began, she came to Mykonos, the island of her origin, and asked its leaders to join.

Then she paid for it. At her own expense she equipped and manned two ships to chase the pirates raiding these islands. And on the 22nd of October 1822, under her leadership, the Mykonians drove off Ottoman troops who had landed here.

It cost her more than money. She sold some of her jewelry to equip 200 men, and she was despised even by her own mother for the choices she made. After the war, Ioannis Kapodistrias gave her the rank of Lieutenant General. Greece became independent in 1830, and she died on Paros in July 1848. From 1988 to 2001, her face was on the two-drachma coin.

This island saw war again in living memory. In September 1944, Greek commandos of the Sacred Squadron raided the German garrison. The remaining German troops surrendered, and the island was free on the 30th of September.

parts.name: Looking for Petros
parts.stand: Stroll along the harbor front, with the water beside you.

paras.t: Keep an eye out along the water. Mykonos has a mascot, a pelican named Petros, and he can sometimes be found at the waterfront, or even up in town.

The first Petros was a great white pelican. Accounts differ on when he arrived: one says he settled here after a storm in 1954, another that a local fisherman found him wounded off the coast in 1958. Either way, he was nursed back to health, the locals looked after him, and the name Petros started as a joke among them.
Sadly, he was hit and killed by a car in December 1985. Afterwards three new pelicans settled around town, and one of them was given his name. So the Petros you meet today is carrying on a title.
If you do meet him, enjoy the moment, but give him space. He's a wild bird, not a pet.

parts.name: Into the lanes
parts.stand: Turn away from the water and step into the narrow lanes behind the harbor.

paras.t: Now the town itself: a maze of tiny whitewashed streets, houses and churches, wrapped around the harbor. Cars aren't allowed in here, so this is a place for walking, and for getting a little lost.
A quick word of care. The lanes are narrow, there are steps where you don't expect them, and the paving can be slick. In the midday heat, take the shady side and keep some water with you.
Notice how many little churches you pass. Wikivoyage counts about 400 on the island. One reason, for many years islanders had to build a church on their land before they could build a house.
The town has grown busy and stylish, but look up from the shop windows and the old Cycladic style is still here, white walls and all.

Some history in these walls. Mykonos came under direct Venetian rule in 1390. Barbarossa's Ottoman fleet attacked in 1537. And right up to the end of the 18th century this was a trading town, drawing newcomers from nearby islands, and drawing pirates too, raid after raid. In June 1794, British and French warships even fought a battle in the island's main harbor.

Even the name is a puzzle, and nobody knows for sure. One old theory says it comes from an ancient Greek word that roughly means a pile of stones. Another ties it to a mythological hero named Mykonos. And myth said the great battle between Zeus and the Giants was fought here, and that the big rocks all over the island are the giants themselves, turned to stone.

parts.name: The three wells
parts.stand: In the middle of town, beside the three wells standing in a row.

paras.t: These three matching wells are Tria Pigadia. They were built in 1722 to give the town its water.
They're shallow, only five or six meters deep, because they were dug into sand, where the water was easier to reach.
So as you wander on, remember the rule about churches: build one for your saint before you build a home for yourself. Whatever you believe, that tells you what these islanders put first.
